case_analysis.focal_point: Whether time spent on supervised release counts toward completing the supervised-release term when the defendant has absconded from supervision, or whether the term is tolled during fugitive status.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 3583 (especially § 3583(i) concerning delayed revocation and the court’s power after the term’s scheduled expiration; also the statutory structure governing commencement/expiration of supervised release).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Rico argues she is entitled to credit for the period her supervised-release term was running on the calendar even though she was not reporting, because Congress did not authorize 'fugitive tolling' for supervised release; § 3583(i) supplies the exclusive mechanism for post-expiration revocation (requiring issuance of a warrant or summons before expiration), and allowing judge-made tolling would improperly expand judicial power beyond the statute’s text and create uncertainty and inequity—particularly given real-world reentry barriers that can lead to nonreporting without a deliberate attempt to evade supervision.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues Rico should not receive credit for time she was a fugitive because absconding defeats the purpose of supervised release; courts should apply a fugitive-tolling principle so a defendant cannot 'run out the clock' by disappearing, and § 3583(i) does not foreclose tolling but instead preserves revocation authority when a warrant/summons issued before expiration—while tolling prevents expiration in the first place during the period the defendant is not actually being supervised.
key_precedents: United States v. Watson (9th Cir. precedent referenced in the district-court transcript concerning fugitive tolling and § 3583(i))

John Roberts.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point—endorsed in various forms in prior cases—is that supervision cannot function during absconding and defendants should not be able to “run out the clock.” But as Justice Barrett persuasively emphasizes, Congress supplied an administrable, textually specified solution in § 3583(i): post-expiration revocation authority depends on a pre-expiration warrant or summons, and a judge-made fugitive-tolling doctrine would largely evade that condition by redefining “expiration” case by case. Justice Thomas’ structural point reinforces the negative inference from § 3624(e): where Congress wanted the clock to stop, it said so, and we should not add an atextual tolling rule that risks consuming the carefully limited mechanism Congress enacted. We can resolve only what is necessary here—absconding alone does not toll the term absent compliance with § 3583(i)—and reserve other potential interruptions for another day.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Government’s best argument is functional: supervised release is supervision, not mere elapsed time, so absconding should suspend the term to prevent a defendant from “running out the clock.” But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Congress already specified when time “does not run” in § 3624(e) and separately set a clear, administrable condition for post-expiration revocation authority in § 3583(i): a warrant or summons issued before expiration. Importing a judge-made fugitive-tolling doctrine would evade that textual prerequisite by redefining “expiration” through an indeterminate, equitable inquiry, effectively enlarging judicial power beyond what Congress granted and rendering § 3583(i)’s limitation largely surplusage. Whatever the policy appeal, our role is to apply the statute as written, not to add an atextual tolling rule that Congress conspicuously omitted.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point—emphasized in various forms as the “no running out the clock” concern—has intuitive appeal, because supervision cannot meaningfully operate while the defendant is a fugitive. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett explain, the statutory structure answers that policy concern through a specific, textually conditioned mechanism: § 3583(i) preserves post-expiration revocation power only when a warrant or summons issues before the term’s expiration, and a judge-made tolling rule would largely evade that condition by redefining “expiration” and rendering § 3583(i)’s trigger partly surplusage. Justice Thomas’ negative-implication point from § 3624(e) reinforces that conclusion: where Congress wanted the clock to stop, it said so, and we are not at liberty to add an extra-textual tolling doctrine in § 3583. The Government’s remedy is prompt process under the scheme Congress enacted, not a judicial enlargement of authority after the calendared term ends.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point remains the functional concern that absconders should not be able to “run out the clock,” but that policy intuition cannot supply authority Congress withheld. As the Chief Justice notes, § 3583(i) provides a precise, administrable mechanism for post-expiration revocation—issuance of a warrant or summons before expiration—and a judge-made fugitive-tolling doctrine would largely evade that express condition by redefining when the term “expires.” Justice Thomas’ structural point about Congress’ explicit “does not run” rule in § 3624(e) reinforces the negative implication: when Congress wanted tolling, it said so, and it conspicuously did not do so for absconding in § 3583. Given those textual choices, we should enforce § 3583(i)’s limits as written rather than adopt an equitable gloss that expands judicial power beyond the statute.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point is functional: supervised release cannot do its work while the defendant is a fugitive, so tolling seems needed to prevent “running out the clock.” But the text and structure supply Congress’s chosen solution—§ 3583(i) extends revocation power past “expiration” only when a warrant or summons issues before that date—and a judicial fugitive-tolling rule would largely evade that condition by redefining “expiration” itself. As Justice Barrett stresses, Congress knew how to write a “does not run” provision (see § 3624(e)), and its omission in § 3583 is a powerful negative implication. And as the Chief notes, replacing § 3583(i)’s administrable trigger with a case-by-case “fugitive” inquiry would both invite indeterminate litigation and render § 3583(i)’s limits partly surplusage.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point remains the practical worry that an absconder can “run out the clock,” but that policy concern cannot displace Congress’s chosen triggers. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 3583(i) supplies an administrable, textually specified condition for post-expiration revocation authority—issuance of a warrant or summons before expiration—and a judge-made fugitive-tolling rule would effectively redefine “expiration” to evade that condition and invite indeterminate litigation over “fugitive” status. Justice Thomas’s structural point reinforces the conclusion: Congress expressly provided a “does not run” rule in § 3624(e), and its omission of any parallel absconding tolling in § 3583 is a negative implication we are not free to “fix” by equity. On the statute’s words and mechanics, the court’s power ends at expiration unless § 3583(i)’s pre-expiration warrant/summons requirement is satisfied.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point—that an absconder should not be able to “run out the clock”—has intuitive force, but it cannot justify grafting an atextual fugitive-tolling doctrine onto § 3583. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Congress specified an administrable trigger in § 3583(i): post-expiration revocation power exists only if a warrant or summons issues before the term’s expiration; fugitive tolling would largely evade that condition by redefining “expiration” through a factbound equitable inquiry. The statutory structure reinforces the negative inference (Justice Thomas): Congress expressly stopped the clock in § 3624(e) for certain imprisonment but did not do so for absconding in § 3583, so we should not supply the missing rule ourselves. Even accepting the policy concern, the statutory scheme channels the Government to timely process under § 3583(i), not to after-the-fact extensions of judicial power.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Respondent’s best point is functional: supervised release cannot achieve its supervisory aims while a defendant is a fugitive, so the term should be treated as suspended to prevent “running out the clock.” But as the Chief Justice notes, Congress supplied a specific, administrable solution in § 3583(i)—a warrant or summons issued before “expiration”—and a judge-made fugitive-tolling doctrine would largely evade that condition by redefining what “expiration” means. The negative implication is reinforced by Congress’s express “does not run” rule in § 3624(e), highlighted by Justice Thomas, showing that when Congress wanted to stop the clock it said so; its different wording in § 3583(i) is a distinction we should respect. And given supervised release’s forward-looking, rehabilitative role (Johnson; Granderson), the statute’s design channels the Government toward prompt process rather than open-ended, equitable extensions of sentencing authority.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point is the equitable and functional one: absconding frustrates supervision, so the term should not be allowed to "run out." But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, Congress addressed that precise timing problem in a textually bounded way—§ 3583(i) preserves revocation authority after the term expires only if a warrant or summons issued before expiration—and a judge-made fugitive-tolling rule would largely evade that administrable trigger by redefining “expiration” through a case-by-case inquiry. The broader structure confirms the negative inference Justice Thomas highlights: Congress expressly stopped the clock in § 3624(e) for specified imprisonment, yet omitted any comparable absconding tolling in § 3583, so we should not add it by equitable gloss. Consistent with supervised release’s forward-looking, statute-specific regime, the remedy for absconding is timely process under § 3583(i), not an atextual expansion of judicial power after the fact.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 3583’s text and structure supply a specific, administrable mechanism for post-expiration revocation in § 3583(i)—conditioning continued judicial authority on the issuance of a warrant or summons before the term’s scheduled expiration—and a judge-made fugitive-tolling rule would largely circumvent that limitation by redefining “expiration” whenever a defendant is not reporting. Reading tolling into the statute risks surplusage by allowing courts to reach cases § 3583(i) already addresses (and limits), and it replaces Congress’s clear trigger (warrant/summons) with an indeterminate inquiry into when nonreporting becomes “fugitive” status. The Government’s policy concerns are real, but they are answered by the statute as written: officers can preserve jurisdiction by timely obtaining a warrant or summons, and we need not decide broader questions about other interruptions of supervision beyond absconding. On these facts, because the Government did not satisfy § 3583(i)’s prerequisite before the scheduled end of Rico’s term, her calendar time counts and the court lacked authority to extend supervision through tolling.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The enacted text does not authorize a judge-made “fugitive tolling” rule for supervised release: Congress specified when a supervised-release term “does not run” in § 3624(e) (imprisonment of 30+ days) and created a distinct, textually bounded mechanism for post-expiration revocation in § 3583(i) that depends on issuance of a warrant or summons before the term’s scheduled expiration. Reading an additional, atextual tolling doctrine into § 3583 would “manufacture ambiguity” and enlarge judicial power to extend supervision beyond the calendar term without the statutory trigger Congress required. On these facts, Rico’s term continued to run absent a statutorily authorized tolling event, so once the term expired the court’s authority depended on strict compliance with § 3583(i), not an equitable time-stop rule. Courts may not create extra-statutory exceptions simply because absconding frustrates supervision; that policy judgment belongs to Congress.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 3583’s structure is textually specific about when a court may act after the scheduled expiration of supervised release: § 3583(i) conditions “[t]he power of the court to revoke” on issuance of a warrant or summons before expiration, thereby supplying the statute’s express, limited mechanism for post-expiration revocation authority. Reading § 3583(i) alongside the rest of § 3583, Congress chose particular tolling/extension devices (e.g., revocation and reimprisonment under § 3583(e)(3), later supervision under § 3583(h), and delayed revocation under § 3583(i)); it did not authorize an additional judge-made “fugitive tolling” rule that would effectively rewrite the expiration date and expand judicial power beyond the conditions Congress imposed. Even if absconding undermines supervised release’s purposes, that policy intuition cannot overcome the statute’s jurisdictional limits and the clarity Congress demanded for sentence-altering actions that remain tethered to the original offense and the specified § 3553(a) factors. On these facts, because Rico’s term continued to run on the calendar absent a statutorily valid extension of power under § 3583(i), she is entitled to credit for that time, and revocation authority after expiration depends strictly on compliance with § 3583(i).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 3583 sets the limits of a court’s revocation authority, and Congress provided an express, textually cabined mechanism for acting after a supervised-release term’s scheduled expiration: § 3583(i) allows delayed revocation only if a warrant or summons issued before expiration. That cross-referenced, enumerated scheme conspicuously omits any authorization to “toll” the term during absconding, and I would not add a judge-made exception that effectively extends the term beyond what the statute says. Applying that structure to Rico’s case, the calendar time counts toward completion absent statutory tolling, and the Government’s policy concern about defendants “running out the clock” must be addressed by Congress (or by timely issuance of a warrant/summons under § 3583(i)), not by judicially expanding the term. Bowles reinforces that courts may not craft equitable workarounds that alter congressionally set limits on judicial power in timing/jurisdictional contexts.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The most natural reading of § 3583’s scheme is that a supervised-release “term” runs for the period the court imposed, unless Congress has specified a statutory mechanism to stop the clock—and here it did not for absconders. Congress did write an express tolling rule elsewhere (e.g., § 3624(e)), and its choice in § 3583(i) to authorize only a narrow, post-expiration revocation power—conditioned on a warrant or summons issued before the term expires—shows that courts may not create a broader judge-made fugitive-tolling exception that bypasses those textual limits. Reading the statute as a whole, fugitive tolling would undercut § 3583(i)’s carefully drawn trigger and timing constraints and expand judicial power to revoke after the scheduled expiration without the required pre-expiration process. Whatever the policy concern about “running out the clock,” Congress addressed late revocation through § 3583(i), and our job is to apply that text to Rico’s abscondment rather than supply an extra-statutory tolling doctrine.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The interpretive task begins with the text Congress enacted, and § 3583(i) specifies the trigger for post-expiration revocation power: before the supervised-release term expires, a warrant or summons must issue; only then may a court act after the scheduled expiration for a reasonably necessary period. Nothing in § 3583 authorizes a judge-made “fugitive tolling” rule that stops the clock whenever a supervisee absconds, and importing that atextual carve-out would rewrite the statute’s carefully drawn timing and power limits. The statutory structure reinforces that conclusion: where Congress wanted tolling in related supervision contexts it said so expressly, and we should not treat silence as an invitation to expand judicial power beyond the conditions Congress set. On these facts, because Rico’s supervised-release term continued to run on the calendar absent an authorized statutory tolling mechanism, the government cannot extend the term (and the court’s revocation power) by equitable invention rather than by satisfying § 3583(i)’s warrant/summons requirement.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: As a matter of statutory text and structure, § 3583 sets a calendar-based term of supervised release that begins upon release and expires at the end of the imposed term, and Congress expressly specified the limited circumstance in which a court’s revocation power extends past that scheduled expiration: § 3583(i) requires that a warrant or summons issue before expiration. Reading the cross-referenced provisions together, Congress provided tolling in § 3624(e) for certain imprisonment, but it did not enact a parallel tolling rule for fugitive status in § 3583—so courts should not add a judge-made tolling doctrine that effectively extends the term and expands the court’s post-expiration authority beyond § 3583(i). That conclusion is reinforced because § 3583(i) speaks in jurisdictional terms (“[t]he power of the court”), and under this Court’s cases courts may not create equitable exceptions that enlarge jurisdictional limits. On these facts, where Rico’s term would have expired absent a timely warrant/summons, the statute does not authorize revocation based on a fugitive-tolling theory.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 3583(i) is an enumerated, conditional grant of "[t]he power of the court" to revoke after the term’s scheduled expiration, and it specifies a single trigger (a warrant or summons issued before expiration); that express list supports a strong negative inference that courts may not create an atextual alternative mechanism—like judge-made “fugitive tolling”—to keep the term from expiring. The whole-statute structure reinforces the point: where Congress wanted to alter how supervised-release time is credited or extended, it did so expressly in § 3583’s neighboring provisions, so the omission of tolling language is a “distinction with a difference.” Consistent usage also matters: § 3583 repeatedly treats the supervised-release “term” as a time-bounded component of the original “sentence,” and § 3583(i) then narrowly preserves revocation authority beyond that term only on specified conditions, not by recharacterizing calendar time as non-time. And because supervised release is forward-looking and rehabilitative (Johnson; Granderson), the statute’s design channels courts toward prompt action (warrant/summons) rather than open-ended, after-the-fact extensions of authority based on equitable assessments of fugitive status.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The text and structure of Congress’s supervised-release scheme do not authorize judge-made “fugitive tolling”: Congress specified one tolling rule in § 3624(e) (imprisonment in connection with a conviction), and it separately addressed post-expiration revocation in § 3583(i) by requiring a warrant or summons issued before the term’s scheduled end. Giving effect to those expressed choices—and to what Congress omitted—means the supervised-release term continues to run on the calendar even if the defendant stops reporting, with the Government’s remedy being timely issuance of a warrant/summons to preserve revocation authority under § 3583(i). Creating an additional tolling doctrine would expand judicial power beyond the statute’s carefully drawn limits and blur the forward-looking supervised-release regime Congress designed. On these facts, because Rico’s term cannot be extended by an extra-textual tolling rule, credit must be given for the period that elapsed absent a statutorily preserved basis for delayed revocation.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a defendant’s supervised-release term continues to run—and thus expires—during periods when the defendant absconds from supervision, or instead is tolled so that the defendant receives no “street-time” credit while a fugitive.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 3583 (especially § 3583(i) (delayed revocation) and the statutory scheme governing commencement/administration of supervised release); related interpretive backdrop includes 18 U.S.C. § 3624(e) (tolling for imprisonment in connection with a conviction), though the Question Presented frames the issue as supervised-release credit during absconding.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Rico argues she is entitled to credit for the time that elapsed on her supervised-release calendar even while she was not reporting (i.e., her term kept running), because Congress specified when supervised release tolls (notably for certain imprisonment) and did not authorize judge-made “fugitive tolling”; allowing tolling would expand federal court power beyond the statute’s text, undermine clear jurisdictional/time limits in the supervised-release framework, and improperly treat absconding as automatically stopping the statutory term absent an express tolling rule enacted by Congress.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues supervised release should not be deemed successfully served while the defendant is a fugitive: absconding prevents supervision from occurring, so the term should be tolled (no credit for “street time” while absconding) and the court may revoke even if the calendar end-date has passed; otherwise, a defendant could evade consequences for violating release conditions (including new criminal conduct) simply by disappearing until the term’s nominal end, frustrating the purposes of supervised release and rewarding flight.
key_precedents: United States v. Watson (9th Cir. precedent referenced in the district-court colloquy; addresses fugitive tolling/supervised-release expiration and Ninth Circuit binding effect)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh make the best practical point: an absconder is not meaningfully being supervised, and it seems perverse to award “street-time” credit for deliberate flight. But that policy intuition cannot supply authority Congress withheld: § 3624(e) contains an express “does not run” rule tied to imprisonment, and § 3583(i) separately preserves revocation power after expiration only if a warrant or summons issues before the term ends. As Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize, adopting a judge-made fugitive-tolling doctrine would sit uneasily with that structure and would dilute § 3583(i)’s timing condition in the very cases where it is meant to matter. The administrable, textually grounded rule is therefore that the term runs absent statutory tolling or a timely warrant/summons under § 3583(i), even if that leaves policy concerns for Congress to address.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh press the strongest point: an absconder is not meaningfully “serving” supervised release, so the term should pause to avoid rewarding flight. But that argument depends on an atextual redefinition of “serving” that effectively manufactures an additional tolling rule beyond the one Congress actually enacted in § 3624(e), and it would loosen § 3583(i)’s express, warrant-or-summons-before-expiration condition by extending the term itself rather than preserving jurisdiction on Congress’s terms. As the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, the statutory structure already calibrates timing and authority; we have no warrant to graft on fugitive tolling simply to reach a more appealing policy outcome. Whatever the incentives, the remedy is faithful application of § 3583(i) (timely process) or legislative amendment—not judicial supplementation.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Barrett press a serious negative-implication point: Congress expressly said in § 3624(e) that supervised release “does not run” during certain imprisonment, and in § 3583(i) it conditioned post-expiration revocation on a timely warrant or summons. But I do not think recognizing fugitive tolling adds a new, free-floating exception; it reflects the ordinary meaning of “serving” supervised release—one cannot be said to be serving a term of supervision while deliberately making supervision impossible. As Justice Kavanaugh notes, § 3583(i) still has substantial work to do for cases where the defendant remains available but proceedings are delayed, so the doctrine does not collapse the statutory limits. And the alternative reading invites the perverse result that a defendant can nullify Congress’s supervision scheme simply by absconding until the calendar runs out, a consequence I cannot attribute to Congress absent clearer text.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh are right to flag the practical concern that an absconder is not meaningfully being supervised, but that policy intuition cannot supply statutory authorization. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Congress specified one circumstance in which supervised release “does not run” in § 3624(e), and it separately cabined post-expiration revocation in § 3583(i) to cases with a pre-expiration warrant or summons—choices that invite a straightforward negative implication against additional, judge-made tolling. Recasting fugitive tolling as merely construing “serving” supervised release still alters the scheme by extending the term itself and thereby diluting § 3583(i)’s express timing boundary in the very cases it is designed to police. If Congress wishes to prevent “street-time credit” for absconders, it can add that tolling rule expressly; we should not adopt a statutory design Congress did not enact.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh make the best practical point: an absconder is not meaningfully being supervised, and it seems perverse to let him “run out the clock.” But that policy intuition can’t displace the textual structure Congress chose—§ 3624(e) says supervised release “does not run” in one specified circumstance (imprisonment in connection with a conviction), and reading “serving” to smuggle in a second, judge-made tolling category is hard to square with that express enumeration. As the Chief Justice emphasized, § 3583(i) is Congress’s targeted mechanism for late or delayed revocation, and fugitive tolling would largely evade its warrant/summons and “reasonably necessary” limits, creating a serious anti-surplusage and whole-scheme problem. If Congress wants absconding to toll, it knows how to say so; we should not revise the scheme under the guise of ordinary meaning.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s best point is the intuitive one: an absconder is not meaningfully being “supervised,” so it seems odd to say he is “serving” supervised release and to award him street-time credit. But Congress addressed exactly when a supervised-release term “does not run” in § 3624(e), and it tied that consequence to imprisonment in connection with a conviction—suggesting by negative implication that other circumstances (including flight) do not stop the clock. As the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas stress, § 3583(i) supplies a separate, formal mechanism for preserving revocation authority past expiration—issuance of a warrant or summons before the term ends—and a judge-made fugitive-tolling rule would effectively expand post-expiration power while diminishing the work Congress assigned that warrant/summons trigger. Policy concerns about perverse incentives are real, but they are for Congress to address by adding an absconding tolling provision, not for us to supply by re-defining “serving” in a way that sidesteps the statute’s carefully drawn conditions.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Thomas’s negative-implication point from § 3624(e) and the carefully conditioned backstop in § 3583(i) is the strongest textual argument against fugitive tolling, and I take seriously the concern about courts adding an atextual “does not run” category. But I continue to think the better reading is not an extra tolling exception but a construction of what it means to be “serving” supervised release: an absconder is not actually undergoing supervised release in any ordinary sense, so the term is not being executed during fugitive status. Section 3583(i) still has independent work in cases where the defendant is available and the Government timely initiates process but adjudication is delayed, so recognizing this limited principle does not collapse Congress’s scheme. As Justice Alito emphasizes, absent that reading the statute would effectively confer an entitlement to defeat supervision by flight, a consequence I am not persuaded Congress enacted in the absence of clear text to that effect.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh are right to emphasize that an absconder is not meaningfully being supervised, and the policy intuition against awarding “street time” has force. But Congress did not leave the question of when supervised release “does not run” to implication; § 3624(e) expressly names one circumstance (imprisonment in connection with a conviction), and under the negative implication that deliberate enumeration is strong evidence against adding an unstated fugitive-tolling category. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, recognizing fugitive tolling would also sit uneasily with § 3583(i)’s carefully cabined post-expiration authority keyed to a pre-expiration warrant or summons, effectively expanding judicial power beyond Congress’s chosen trigger. Whatever the practical concern, the statutory scheme supplies an administrable mechanism, and it is not our role to treat Congress’s omission as a drafting mistake.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is the common-sense claim that an absconder is not meaningfully “serving” supervised release, and that letting the calendar run rewards flight and undermines supervised release’s rehabilitative and public-safety aims. But that policy intuition cannot supply what Congress conspicuously omitted: a fugitive-tolling rule—especially where Congress expressly provided a “does not run” rule in § 3624(e) and separately calibrated the only post-expiration revocation mechanism in § 3583(i) to a pre-expiration warrant or summons and a “reasonably necessary” time limit. As the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett explain, importing judge-made tolling would effectively extend supervision and bypass § 3583(i)’s conditions, diluting the statutory scheme’s timing limits in the very cases they are designed to constrain. Whatever the practical concern about ‘street-time credit,’ the statute’s text and structure indicate the remedy is timely process under § 3583(i) or legislative amendment, not judicial addition.

John Roberts.reasoning: Start with the statute’s text and structure: Congress expressly provided one tolling rule for supervised release in § 3624(e) (tolling during imprisonment “in connection with a conviction”), and it separately enacted § 3583(i) to confer a limited, post-expiration “delayed revocation” jurisdiction only when a warrant or summons issues before the term ends. Reading an additional, judge-made “fugitive tolling” doctrine into § 3583 would add a tolling mechanism Congress did not include and would risk rendering § 3583(i)’s carefully drawn timing limits largely superfluous, contrary to whole-statute coherence and anti-surplusage principles. The Government’s policy concerns are substantial, but administrability cuts the other way where the statute already supplies a straightforward, workaday rule: the term runs as imposed, with tolling only where Congress said so and with post-term jurisdiction only under § 3583(i)’s conditions. On these facts, if the Government did not secure a warrant or summons before the supervised-release calendar expired, the court’s revocation power cannot be extended by an extra-textual tolling doctrine.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The enacted text supplies the relevant tolling rule and it is limited: § 3624(e) expressly stops supervised release only when the defendant is imprisoned in connection with a conviction, and nothing in § 3583 creates an additional, judge-made “fugitive tolling” doctrine for absconders. Reading the statutory scheme as a whole, Congress addressed timing/jurisdiction at the end of the term in § 3583(i) by allowing delayed revocation only if a warrant or summons issues before the term’s expiration—an administrable, textual limit that courts may not evade by inventing extra-statutory tolling. The Government’s policy concerns cannot justify using supervisory power or atextual equitable doctrines to add an exception Congress did not enact; if flight warrants a broader tolling rule, Congress knows how to write one, as it did elsewhere (e.g., § 3290). On these facts, because petitioner’s term ran by the calendar and no statutory tolling provision applies to her period of absconding, the supervised-release term continued to run and expired absent a timely warrant or summons under § 3583(i).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Reading § 3583 as a practical, administrable scheme, a defendant cannot be said to be “serving” supervised release while deliberately absconding and making supervision impossible; the statutory term should therefore be understood to stop running during fugitive status so the defendant receives no street-time credit. That interpretation best fits the purposes Congress assigned supervised release—rehabilitation and protection of the public through monitoring—and avoids the perverse consequence that a defendant can defeat enforcement simply by disappearing until the calendar end-date. Section 3583(i) is properly read as a backstop for delayed revocation when the term would otherwise expire; recognizing fugitive tolling does not create a free-floating equitable exception but rather applies a common-sense rule that the supervised-release “term” is not being executed when the defendant is a fugitive. On these facts—where Rico stopped reporting and remained at large—the District Court retained authority to revoke and impose a sanction without rewarding flight.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Congress specified when supervised release does not run by enacting an express tolling rule in § 3624(e) (imprisonment in connection with a conviction) and, in § 3583(i), separately cabined the court’s power to revoke after expiration to situations where a warrant or summons issued before the term ended. The straightforward negative implication from those deliberate choices is that courts lack authority to create an additional, judge-made “fugitive tolling” category that stops the clock whenever a defendant absconds—particularly because doing so would expand judicial power beyond the express limits Congress set for post-expiration revocation. The Government’s policy concerns about rewarding flight invite speculation about a statutory design Congress could have enacted but did not; the statute instead addresses absconding through violation proceedings and the jurisdictional mechanism of timely warrants/summonses, not by rewriting the term’s duration. Because the supervised-release scheme is a tightly structured, time-bound regime, courts must adhere to Congress’s express authorizations and cannot add equitable exceptions that effectively extend supervised release and revocation jurisdiction.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The most natural reading of the statutory text is that supervised release runs continuously once it “commences,” except where Congress expressly said it “does not run”—and § 3624(e) contains a tolling rule only for imprisonment in connection with a conviction, not for absconding. Reading a judge-made “fugitive tolling” rule into § 3583 would sit uneasily with the statute’s broader structure, because Congress already calibrated the consequences of late-discovered violations through § 3583(i)’s limited delayed-revocation authority; allowing tolling for flight would effectively rewrite that jurisdictional backstop and expand revocation power beyond the conditions Congress specified. The whole-scheme fit and anti-surplusage cross-check point the same way: if absconding automatically tolls, § 3583(i)’s warrant/summons mechanism and its time limits do less independent work, because courts could extend supervision simply by deeming the term paused. Whatever the policy appeal of denying “street time” to fugitives, that is for Congress to enact, as it did in § 3624(e)’s specific tolling clause.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Start with the text Congress enacted. Section 3624(e) specifies one circumstance in which a supervised-release term “does not run” (imprisonment in connection with a conviction), and § 3583(i) supplies a separate, tightly drawn mechanism for “delayed revocation” after expiration only when a warrant or summons issues before the term ends—none of which speaks to tolling for absconding. Reading an additional, judge-made “fugitive tolling” rule into the statute would effectively rewrite the statute’s triggers for stopping the clock and enlarge the court’s revocation power beyond the formal conditions Congress prescribed, especially given § 3583(i)’s emphasis on timely process (warrant/summons) as the jurisdiction-preserving event. Whatever the policy concerns about rewarding flight, the statutory scheme reflects Congress’s choice to address timing through specified tolling and specified pre-expiration process, and our job is to apply those enacted conditions to Rico’s absconding, not to add new ones.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The starting point is the Court’s supervised-release framework and the controlling statutory structure: supervised release is designed to be actual supervision, not a mere passage of calendar time, and § 3583(i) already supplies a clear, administrable trigger for delayed revocation when a warrant or summons issues before the term otherwise would expire. Applying the Court’s doctrine-driven approach, the question is whether Congress’s scheme leaves room for a background rule that a defendant cannot run out the clock by absconding; in light of this Court’s recognition that supervised release serves rehabilitative and public-safety functions, a fugitive cannot be credited with “street time” during which supervision is impossible. The alternative rule would create perverse incentives and disrupt settled lower-court practice (including longstanding Ninth Circuit precedent) by allowing defendants to nullify supervision simply by disappearing until the nominal end date. Consistent with stability and administrability, I would not read § 3583 to confer an entitlement to credit for time spent as a fugitive absent actual supervision, and would affirm the revocation here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text and structure of the supervised-release scheme supply a strong negative implication against judge-made “fugitive tolling”: Congress expressly provided for tolling in § 3624(e) (imprisonment in connection with a conviction), and it separately enacted a carefully delimited delayed-revocation mechanism in § 3583(i), conditioning “the power of the court to revoke” on issuance of a warrant or summons before the term’s expiration. Reading an additional, unwritten tolling rule for absconding would treat Congress’s selective drafting as a mistake and would effectively expand the court’s power beyond the jurisdictional boundary Congress set in § 3583(i). Intrastatutory context reinforces that supervised release is a component of the original sentence with a fixed term that runs according to statute, not an open-ended supervisory entitlement that can be paused whenever supervision is imperfect. Whatever policy concerns about rewarding flight, they cannot overcome Congress’s choice to enumerate when supervised release stops running and how revocation may proceed after expiration.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The statutory question is whether Congress authorized courts to stop the supervised-release clock when a defendant absconds, and the text and structure indicate it did not. Congress expressly provided one tolling rule in § 3624(e) (imprisonment in connection with a conviction) and, through that conspicuous omission, signaled that additional judge-made tolling (including “fugitive tolling”) is not permitted. Section 3583(i) further confirms the scheme Congress chose for absconding-related edge cases: the court retains revocation power after the term’s scheduled expiration only if a warrant or summons issued before expiration and only for a reasonably necessary period—limitations that fugitive tolling would effectively bypass. However problematic “street-time credit” during flight may seem as a policy matter, Congress addressed that concern through § 3583(i)’s warrant-and-timing mechanism, and courts should not expand their authority beyond what the supervised-release statutes affirmatively authorize.
